newsitem.title: CHINA: China long way from WTO entry as chief due to visit.
newsitem.headline: China long way from WTO entry as chief due to visit.

text.p: China is gearing for the first visit by World Trade Organisation chief Renato Ruggiero but diplomats said numerous problems still hamper its long-delayed application for entry with Beijing making few concessions.
"China still has a very long way to go," one European diplomat said on Wednesday.
"There are few signs of desperation or that they have the ability to do anything radical to get in," he said. "A lot of barriers remain and whether they can pull it off this year is still doubtful."

Ruggiero, arriving in Shanghai on Friday for a six-day visit to China, was expected to try to find ways to accelerate China's admission, with the WTO chief seen taking the opportunity to stress to China's leaders the advantages of membership.
Diplomats from countries involved in bilateral talks with China on its applications said Ruggiero faced a tough task.
"Ruggiero can keep the momentum going," the diplomat said.
"He can help the process of persuading China's ministries that joining the WTO will be beneficial for China," he said. "But a lot of work needs to be done internally to raise awareness."

Other Western diplomats said they had seen little change in China's position, citing a need for Beijing to lift a wide range of barriers including opening its agriculture markets, financial services, trading rights and distribution systems as well as clarifying controversial subsidies to state industry.

Ruggiero said last month that China was now approaching the final stages of an entry process to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and its successor organisation the WTO that has already taken a decade.
Diplomats in Beijing were less sanguine.
"There has been no sign of a change in their position," said the Western diplomat despite statements by Chinese negotiators that they had made progress in recent talks in Geneva.
Agreement has been reached on the principle that China will be allowed to enter under a phased system that would give it time to introduce reforms over a certain period.
"But there has to be a real downpayment," said another diplomat. "They want to get in on the basis of not making too many changes, but we have to have set assurances."

Areas where China has yet to meet demands from Europe, Japan and the United States include trading rights -- allowing foreign firms to engage in imports and exports in China -- and national treatment on distribution.

Other China monopolies that unite developed nations in negotiations with Beijing are financial services -- prising open the insurance and banking sectors -- as well as accounting, law firms, education and tourism and travel.

One German survey showed that China's much-vaunted slashing of import tariffs to an average of 23 percent from 35 percent was in fact of greater benefit to foreign consumers than to Chinese consumers.

The United States was looking for movement on China's agricultural health barriers, saying these affected a slew of products from citrus to wheat to tobacco, pork and chicken and had drawn the ire of congressmen nationwide.

China's slow opening of its markets was another area of contention -- with U.S. import growth to China up just 0.2 percent in 1996 viewed as disappointing when China's economy skyrocketed by 10 percent, Western diplomats said.

Beijing's arguments that U.S. limits on high technology exports hampered exports did not hold water since imports from Japan grew just 0.2 percent and those from Europe fell 6.5 percent but neither region limits exports, diplomats said.
Diplomats hinted at a battle of wills.
"The longer the Chinese stay out of the WTO rules making process, the worse off they are," said one diplomat.

"The U.S. price is too high," said Niu Jun, a researcher on Sino-U.S. ties at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. "It is more difficult to forecast whether China can enter by the end of the year, but there is hope."
